content: An infant, in basic terms, is defined as a human child in the earliest stage of life, typically before they can walk and generally under the age of one. The word infant originates from the Latin term in-fans, meaning unable to speak. There is no universally agreed-upon definition of infancy. In legal contexts, infant can also refer to a minor, meaning any child under the age of legal adulthood. A human infant less than one month old is referred to as a newborn or neonate. The term newborn encompasses premature infants, postmature infants, and full-term newborns. Once infants reach the age of one or begin walking, they are often referred to as toddlers, typically between 12 and 36 months of age. In daycare settings, children in the infant room may still be called infants even if they are older than one year or walking, with some facilities using the term walking infant. The Newborn Appearance A newborn's shoulders and hips are narrow, the abdomen protrudes slightly, and the arms and legs are relatively short. The average weight of a newborn is approximately 3.4 kg (7.5 lbs), and the average length is about 50.8 cm (20 inches), though premature newborns may be significantly smaller. The Apgar score is used to assess a newborn's transition from the uterus during the first minutes of life. A newborn's head is disproportionately large compared to the rest of the body, with the cranium being significantly larger relative to the face. While an adult human skull is about one-eighth of the total body length, a newborn's skull is about one-fourth. At birth, many areas of the newborn's skull have not yet ossified, leaving soft spots known as fontanels. The two largest fontanels are the diamond-shaped anterior fontanel at the top front of the head and the smaller triangular-shaped posterior fontanel at the back of the head. These bones will naturally fuse later in the child's life. A protein called noggin is responsible for delaying the fusion of an infant's skull. During labor and delivery, the infant's skull may change shape to pass through the birth canal, sometimes resulting in a misshapen or elongated head. This typically resolves on its own within a few days or weeks, though physicians may recommend specific exercises to aid the process. Some newborns have fine, downy body hair called lanugo, which is especially noticeable on the back, shoulders, forehead, ears, and face of premature infants. Lanugo usually disappears within a few weeks. Not all infants are born with a full head of hair; some may be nearly bald, while others may have very fine, almost invisible hair. Some babies are even born with a full head of hair. Among fair-skinned parents, this fine hair may be blond, even if the parents themselves are not. The scalp of a newborn may also be temporarily bruised or swollen, particularly in hairless newborns, and the area around the eyes may appear puffy. Immediately after birth, a newborn's skin is often grayish or dusky blue in color. Once the newborn begins breathing, usually within a minute or two, the skin color returns to its normal tone. Newborns are typically wet, covered in streaks of blood, and coated with a white substance called vernix caseosa, which is believed to act as an antibacterial barrier. Newborns may also have Mongolian spots, various other birthmarks, or peeling skin, particularly on the wrists, hands, ankles, and feet. A newborn's genitals are often enlarged and reddened, with male infants having an unusually large scrotum. The breasts may also be enlarged in both male and female infants due to naturally occurring maternal hormones, a temporary condition. Female infants (and occasionally males) may discharge milk from their nipples (sometimes called witch's milk) or a bloody or milky-like substance from the vagina. These occurrences are normal and will resolve over time. The umbilical cord of a newborn is bluish-white in color. After birth, the cord is typically cut, leaving a 1–2 inch stub. The umbilical stub will dry out, shrivel, darken, and fall off within about three weeks. Hospitals may occasionally apply triple dye to the umbilical stub to prevent infection, which may temporarily color the stub and surrounding skin purple. Newborns lose many of these physical characteristics quickly, and older babies often look very different. While older babies are often considered cute, newborns may be perceived as unattractive by the same standards, and first-time parents may need to be educated about this. The Newborn's Senses Newborns can perceive a variety of sensations but respond most positively to soft stroking, cuddling, and caressing. Gentle rocking back and forth often soothes a crying infant, as do massages and warm baths. Newborns may self-soothe by sucking their thumb or a pacifier. The instinct to suckle is innate and enables newborns to feed. Newborns have limited vision and can focus on objects only about 18 inches (45 cm) directly in front of their face. This distance is sufficient for the infant to look at the mother's eyes or areola during breastfeeding. Generally, a newborn cries when hungry. When not sleeping, feeding, or crying, newborns may spend time staring at random objects, particularly those that are shiny, have sharp contrasting colors, or feature complex patterns. However, newborns show a preference for looking at human faces above all else. While in the womb, the infant could hear many internal sounds, such as the mother's heartbeat, as well as external noises, including human voices, music, and other sounds. Therefore, although a newborn's ears may have some fluid or catarrh, they can hear sounds from before birth. Newborns typically respond more to a female voice than a male voice, which may explain why people instinctively raise the pitch of their voice when speaking to newborns. The sound of human voices, especially the mother's, can have a calming or soothing effect on the newborn. Conversely, loud or sudden noises may startle and frighten a newborn. Newborns can also respond to different tastes, including sweet, sour, bitter, and salty substances, with a preference for sweet tastes. A newborn's sense of smell is developed at birth, and within the first week of life, they can distinguish between their mother's breast milk and that of another female. Infant Mortality Infant mortality refers to the death of an infant within the first year of life. It can be categorized into neonatal death, which occurs within the first 27 days of life, and post-neonatal death, which occurs after 28 days of life. Major causes of infant mortality include dehydration, infection, congenital malformations, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). This epidemiological indicator is considered a critical measure of a country's healthcare quality, as it is directly linked to the health status of infants, children, and pregnant women, as well as access to medical care, socioeconomic conditions, and public health practices. Care and Feeding Infants cry as a basic instinctive form of communication. A crying infant may be expressing hunger, discomfort, overstimulation, boredom, or loneliness. Many caregivers use baby monitors or baby cameras to hear or see an infant's cries from another room. Feeding is typically done through breastfeeding, which is recommended by all major infant health organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics. If breastfeeding is not possible or desired, bottle feeding with expressed breast milk or infant formula may be used. Infants have a natural sucking instinct that allows them to extract milk from the nipples of the breast or a baby bottle, as well as an instinctive rooting behavior to seek out the nipple. In rare cases, a wet nurse may be hired to feed the infant, though this is uncommon, especially in developed countries. As infants grow and their appetites increase, many parents choose from a variety of commercial, ready-made baby foods to supplement breast milk or formula, while others adapt their usual meals to meet the dietary needs of their child. Infants are incontinent, so diapers are commonly used in industrialized countries, while methods similar to elimination communication are more common in developing countries. Practitioners of these techniques assert that babies can control their bodily functions by six months of age and are aware of urination even earlier. Babies can learn to signal to their parents when they need to urinate or defecate by turning or making noises. Parents must pay close attention to the baby's actions to learn these signals. Children require a relatively large amount of sleep to function properly, with newborns sleeping up to 18 hours a day, though this decreases as the child ages. Infants cannot walk, though more mature infants may crawl or scoot. Baby transport may involve strollers, carriers, slings, or simply being carried in the arms. Most industrialized countries have laws requiring infants to be placed in special child safety seats when in motor vehicles. Like most young children, infants are often treated as special individuals. Their social presence differs from that of adults, and they may be the focus of attention. Fees for transportation and entrance to locations such as amusement parks or museums are often waived for infants. However, this special attention diminishes as the child grows older. Common care issues for infants include baby colic, gas, childhood development, hygiene (bathing, cord care), daycare, diaper rash, feeding (breastfeeding or formula), immunization, paternal bonding, pacifier use, sleep (bassinet or infant bed), and teething.
